scorecard.name: Workers using generative AI at work
scorecard.detail: Share of employed adults aged 18–64 who used generative AI for work in the past week, St. Louis Fed survey, Jul 2026, down from 45% in the reading before. Survey readings bounce, so the trend below averages two. Highest in computer and math jobs (69%) and management (63%); lower in office support (37%) and transportation (24%). Time it saves equals about 2.1% of all hours worked, by users' own estimates.

trend.text: Average of the last two readings: 42.9%, up from 36.2% a year earlier

scorecard.name: Tech investment relative to payroll
scorecard.detail: Business spending on information-processing equipment (computers, communications gear and instruments) and software, as a share of total employee pay, Q3 2026. Before 2023 the peak was 8.1% (Q2 2022). Much of the recent jump is data-center building, and these are dollar figures, so part of the rise is prices.

trend.text: Latest: 10.7%, up from 9.0% a year earlier

scorecard.name: Tech equipment investment (inflation-adjusted)
scorecard.detail: Real spending on information-processing equipment over the past year to Q3 2026. Imports of computers rose 62%, so much of it is built abroad. More machines can lift output per hour without any efficiency gain.

trend.text: Growth over the past year: 29.1%, up from 20.8% a year earlier

scorecard.group: Work: are jobs and pay shifting?
scorecard.name: Young graduates' job-finding edge
scorecard.detail: Change since Dec 2023 in how much better college graduates aged 20–24 do than all 20–24-year-olds (unemployment, 12-month averages, to Sep 2026). Graduates now average 6.7% against 7.4%, an edge of 0.7 points; it was 0.9 at the end of 2023, already smaller than in any month of 2002–19. Narrowing of 0.2 points over 33 months: 63% of same-length stretches from Sep 2004 to Dec 2019 narrowed as much. That is within normal noise (above 20%). The edge also swings with the business cycle.

trend.text: Graduates' edge: 0.7 pts, down from 1.4 pts a year earlier

scorecard.group: Work: are jobs and pay shifting?
scorecard.name: Jobs in computer systems design
scorecard.detail: Change since Dec 2023, to Sep 2026, against +1.5% for all private jobs; information jobs −7.6%. The gap with all private jobs (−5.3 points) was as bad in 11% of same-length stretches from Oct 2002 to Dec 2019, all of them right after the dot-com bust. That is suggestive (between 5% and 20%), not yet clear. Tech hiring also slumped in 2023 as interest rates rose, before most firms used AI.

trend.text: Gap vs all private jobs: -5.3 pts, up from -6.1 pts a year earlier

scorecard.group: Work: are jobs and pay shifting?
scorecard.name: Management, business & financial pay vs office support
scorecard.detail: Change since late 2023 in median weekly pay of management, business and financial workers relative to office and administrative support workers, to Q3 2026. One theory (Imas, Koh and Legg, 2026) predicts people who coordinate work gain while routine specialists lose; this group mixes managers with accountants and analysts, so it is a rough proxy. So far office pay has grown faster (4.1% a year vs 3.8%), the opposite. That is within normal noise (above 20%).

scorecard.name: Output per hour, nonfarm business
scorecard.detail: Since the end of 2023, against 1.6% in 2004–19. Given how noisy quarterly data are, chance alone would produce a gap this large about 10% of the time. That is suggestive (between 5% and 20%), not yet clear.

trend.text: Growth over the past year: 2.1%, down from 2.7% a year earlier

scorecard.name: Output per hour, nonfinancial corporations
scorecard.detail: Since the end of 2023, against 1.4% in 2004–19. Given how noisy quarterly data are, chance alone would produce a gap this large about 18% of the time. That is suggestive (between 5% and 20%), not yet clear. This measure leaves out the self-employed and the harder-to-measure parts of the economy.

trend.text: Growth over the past year: 3.6%, up from 2.2% a year earlier

scorecard.name: Income-side check
scorecard.detail: Real income (GDI) minus real output (GDP) growth. GDI has grown 2.7% a year since end-2023, against 2.4% for GDP, through Q2 2026. Income is keeping pace, so output isn't obviously overstated.

scorecard.name: Underlying efficiency (SF Fed)
scorecard.detail: Since end-2023, after removing more machines, more skills and working harder (average of the SF Fed's quarterly figures), against 0.6% a year in 2004–19 and about 2.1% in the 1997–2003 boom. It is below its 2004–19 pace. That is within normal noise (above 20%).

scorecard.name: Official TFP (BLS, annual)
scorecard.detail: 2023–2025, against 0.7% in 2004–19 and 1.5% in 1997–2003. No adjustment for working harder, so it overstates efficiency in a hot economy.

trend.text: Growth in 2025: 0.8%, down from 1.5% a year earlier

scorecard.name: Working harder (factory hours)
scorecard.detail: Weekly hours of factory production workers, Sep 2026, against 40.8 two years earlier (2018 peak 42.4). A quick gauge of whether a hot economy is making people work harder; the SF Fed's adjustment uses a broader set of hours across industries.

trend.text: Latest: 42.0 hrs, up from 41.0 hrs a year earlier

scorecard.name: AI users vs hands-on industries
scorecard.detail: How much more professional & business services sped up than retail, leisure and construction, each measured against its own 2010–19 pace. 6% of 2010–19 stretches showed a gap at least as large, and dropping any one hands−on industry leaves +1.1 pts. That is suggestive (between 5% and 20%), not yet clear.

trend.text: Gap: 1.8 pts, up from 0.3 pts a year earlier

scorecard.name: AI producers: information
scorecard.detail: Speed−up in output per hour since end−2023 against its own 2010–19 pace, bigger than in any 2010–19 stretch (max +2.8). This industry includes data centers and software publishers, which build and sell AI, so it shows AI production rather than use.

scorecard.name: Workers' share of business income
scorecard.detail: Change in labor's share of nonfarm business income since the end of 2023, against −0.4% a year in 2004–19. It is the lowest on record (the series begins in 1947). Chance alone would produce a decline this fast about 35% of the time. That is within normal noise (above 20%). The share is pay per hour divided by output per hour, so a quarter of fast productivity growth pulls it down until pay catches up; it fell from 94.4 to 93.7 last quarter. If machines substitute for people, more of the gains go to owners of capital.

scorecard.name: New businesses likely to hire
scorecard.detail: High-propensity business applications, 12-month average to Sep 2026, against 155k at the end of 2023 and 110k in 2019. A wave of lean AI-native startups would show up here.

scorecard.name: Inflation-adjusted interest rates
scorecard.detail: 10-year TIPS yield on 2026-11-04. Markets tend to push this up when they expect faster growth, but deficits and Fed policy move it too. In the late-1990s boom it was about 3.5–4.5% (Klein's estimate).

trend.text: Oct 2026 average: 2.8%, up from 1.8% a year earlier
